summary: Kwangsoo Park is a scholar of Buddhist and religious studies. He completed an MA at the University of Iowa, earned a PhD at the University of Wisconsin-Madison, and served as a professor at Wonkwang University (attested 2020).

Kyo Kano studied Indology and philosophy, attending Keio University (until 1980), Kyoto University (attested 1987), and the University of Vienna (attested 1987). Kano served as an assistant at Kyoto University (attested 1989) and associate professor at Kobe Women's University (attested 2000).

Buddhist studies scholar Kyojun Shimizutani (1891–1979) studied under Keijun Shimizutani and attended Tendai Sect University and Taisho University. He taught at Tendai Sect University and Taisho University (1926–1945), and served as head priest of Senso-ji (~1952–1979).

Kyoko Amano is a scholar of Indology and linguistics who earned an MPhil from Osaka University and a doctorate from the University of Freiburg (1997–2001). She held various academic posts at Osaka University and Kyoto University (2013–2024).

Kyoko Fujii studied at the University of Tokyo (~1968–1976), working in Buddhist studies and Indology. She was a professor at Hokkaido University (~1996–2013) and the International College for Postgraduate Buddhist Studies, later serving as Director of the International Institute for Buddhist Studies (~2017).

Kyoko Tokuno is a scholar of Buddhist studies and Sinology who taught Douglas Ober. She held posts at the University of Oregon and the University of Washington, where she was an attested professor in 2017.

Kyokuga Saeki (1828–1891) was a Buddhist studies and philosophy scholar who studied under numerous traditional teachers, including Reiga and Gen'yū. He served as the 143rd elder at Sennyu-ji (~1887–1891) and taught Shundo Sugihara, Eto Senabe, and Eto Sebe.

Kyosho Hayashima (1914–1999) was a Buddhist studies and Indology scholar who taught Shinjo Kawasaki and Fumihiko Sueki. His academic posts included lecturer at Yokohama City University (attested 1962) and professor at the University of Tokyo (attested 1980).
Kyosho Tanaka studied Buddhist studies at the University of Tokyo from circa 1966 to 1974. He served as an associate professor at Musashino University from circa 1975 to 2017.
Kyoshun Todo (1916–2002) was a Buddhist studies scholar. He held academic posts at Bukkyo University, serving as an assistant professor (attested 1962) and later as a professor (attested 1988–1992).

Kyozo Yamada (1907–1989), a Buddhist and religious studies scholar, studied at Tokyo Imperial University (~1927–1930) and under several traditional masters, including Sokan Kono. He founded Kamakura Haku-un-kai and became the second head of Sanbo Zen in 1970.

Kyōtarō Nishikawa (1929–2023) studied at Keio University (~1949–1953) and specialized in history, archaeology, Japanology, and Buddhist studies. He was Director-General of the Tokyo National Research Institute for Cultural Properties (~1990–1996) and held a post at Kanagawa Prefectural Museum of Cultural History (~1996–2012).

Károly Fiók (1857–1915) was an Indology scholar who studied at Eötvös Loránd University, the University of Berlin, and the University of Munich. He taught at Budapest Reformed High School (1886–1907) and Debrecen Reformed College (1907–1915).
Käthe Marschner worked in the field of Indology. She studied at the University of Breslau, where she completed her PhD under doctoral supervisor Otto Strauss circa 1929 to 1933.

Käthe Neumann (1903–1989) specialized in religious studies, Indology, and Buddhist studies, earning her PhD at the University of Marburg (~1928–1933) under Johannes Nobel. From 1937 to 1968, she served as curator in charge at the Religionskundliche Sammlung.

Kārlis Augusts Tennisons (1873–1962) was a Buddhist studies figure who studied at Saint Petersburg State University (~1893–1897). He served as director of Datsan Gunzechoinei from 1906 to 1923 and taught Friedrich V. Lustig.

Kōgi Kudara (1945–2004) was a scholar of Buddhist studies, Iranian and Central Asian studies, and linguistics. He served as a professor at Ryukoku University (~1978–2004), worked for the Ryukoku Buddhist Society, and taught Yutaka Kanazawa.
Kōichi Kozaka is a scholar in Buddhist studies and Tibetology who studied under Hakuyu Hadano. He held a post as professor at Osaka Kyoiku University (attested 1991).

Kōsen Imakita (1816–1892) was a Buddhist studies and philosophy scholar who studied under Togai Fujisawa, Kyokuso Hirose, Daisetsu Jōen, and Gisan Zenkai. He served as abbot at Eikō-ji and Engaku-ji (1875–1892), and taught Daisetsu Teitaro Suzuki and Soyen Shaku.
Kōshō Ōtani (1911–2002) was a Buddhist studies figure who studied at First Higher School (~1929–1932) and Tokyo Imperial University (~1932–1935). He succeeded Kozui Otani.
